patches.summary: G4372 πρόσφατος (prosphatos) literally means “freshly slain” (from pro + sphazo, “to slaughter”). Every major translation renders it simply as “new,” obscuring the sacrificial imagery. The same word ζῶσαν (“living”) appears in Romans 12:1 (“living sacrifice”), creating a deliberate paradox: the way is simultaneously freshly-slaughtered and alive — just as believers are called to be living sacrifices.

H1605 gaar is translated 'rebuke' in 11 of its 13 occurrences (including Mal 3:11 one chapter later). Malachi 2:3 is the only place the KJV renders it 'corrupt.' And H6569 peresh ('dung') is not generic manure — every other use in Scripture is the intestinal waste of a sin offering that must be burned outside the camp (Ex 29:14, Lev 4:11, 16:27). God will smear the sacrificial offal of their corrupt feasts on their faces, and they will be carried away with it — treated like the waste of a sacrifice, removed from the camp.

patches.summary: H5671 avtit — Strong's defines as 'something pledged, pawned goods' and flags the KJV's 'thick clay' as a false etymology. From H5670 avat = 'to pawn, to lend on security, to borrow.' The verse warns of a nation loading itself with burdensome debts, whose creditors rise up suddenly.
